extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of theology, biblical exegesis, and political/political-theological philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for determining the proper meaning of ambiguous terms in the Bible (e.g., 'spirit', 'angel', 'inspiration', 'kingdom of God') and for using those determinations in theological and political argument. Emphasizes lexical/contextual analysis of scripture with scriptural examples and consequences for political theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant signification of words in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation of all true reasoning about Scripture is the constant signification of words; meanings used in theological argument should depend on the sense those words carry in Scripture rather than the writer's private will or vulgar usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before inferring from scriptural passages, determine the biblical meaning of ambiguous words. Treat this semantic determination as the necessary starting point for any further doctrinal or political conclusions; where Scripture supplies a sense, use it rather than metaphoric or popular senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body/Substance defined for scriptural interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Body' (or 'substance') in Scripture most generally signifies that which occupies room or place and is part of the aggregate Universe; it is that which undergoes changes (accidents) perceivable by the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret attributions of motion, place, and change in Scripture as implying corporeality unless context compels otherwise. Avoid accepting phrases that imply 'incorporeal substance' without checking for category error (e.g., 'incorporeal body' is contradictory). Use the notion of bodies as things with dimensions and parts when Scripture attributes spatial or mutable qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common usages of 'spirit' (non-technical)
rubrics_metrics.description: In common speech 'spirit' can mean a subtle, fluid, invisible body (aerial substance), a ghost/phantasm of the imagination, or metaphoric dispositions and abilities (e.g., spirit of wisdom, spirit of contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering 'spirit' in Scripture, catalogue which common sense is in play: physical/aerial, imaginal/phantasm, or metaphorical disposition. Use surrounding context and effects attributed to the 'spirit' to disambiguate (e.g., if touch detects nothing, might be a phantasm; if effects are public and shared, may be bodily).

rubrics_metrics.name: If no biblical sense suffices, rely on faith/submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Where none of the identified meanings of a term can satisfactorily explain a scriptural passage, the meaning may be beyond human understanding; faith and submissive assent to Scripture, not speculative opinion, is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent speculative senses when the textual context yields no clear human-understandable meaning; treat such passages as matters of faith rather than objects of further rational disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit understood as wind or breath
rubrics_metrics.description: When Scripture attributes motion or diminution/abating of waters or similar physical effects to 'the Spirit of God', interpret 'spirit' as wind/breath (an aerial substance) rather than God himself or an incorporeal entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel places (e.g., Gen.1:2 and Gen.8:1) to read 'spirit' as a natural, moving air when motion/place is described. Prefer a physical explanation when the description fits natural phenomena (wind diminishing waters, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as extraordinary gift of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spirit of God' can denote extraordinary intellectual gifts (wisdom, understanding, ability), as when Scripture praises persons 'filled with the spirit of wisdom' for special faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read references to 'spirit' accompanying wise or skillful action (e.g., Joseph in Pharaoh's court, artisans consecrated for work in Exodus, Isaiah's list) as indicators of divinely granted capacities rather than literal indwelling incorporeal substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as extraordinary affection or zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Old Testament examples (e.g., Judges, Saul) 'spirit' denotes an extraordinary zeal, courage, or fury prompting decisive action in defense or devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Scripture portrays sudden moral or martial fervor as 'the spirit' coming upon someone, understand it as heightened affection or passion that explains the behavior, not as possession by a ghostly being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as prophetic gift (dreams and visions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic knowledge described as 'by the Spirit of God' is commonly a grant of prediction via supernatural dreams or visions rather than speech by a ghost within the prophet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between prophecy as a vision/dream-mediated disclosure and notions of an inner ghost speaking. Interpret prophetic 'spirit' passages in light of the modes of revelation (dreams, visions) described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as life (vital breath)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spirit' is sometimes used to signify life or vital motion (e.g., 'breath of life'); in such cases it simply denotes that a living condition or vital power is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Scripture uses 'spirit' where the parallel sense is 'life' or 'breath' (e.g., God breathed into Adam), read it as a metaphor for God giving life, not as the infusion of a separable divine substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as subordination to authority or doctrinal submission
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spirit' can signify being under an authority or adhering to a doctrine (e.g., being 'full of the spirit' because ordained by a superior; confessing Christ 'in the flesh' as evidence of a spirit being of God).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such usages as indicating delegated authority, ordination, or genuine conformity to essential Christian doctrine, rather than metaphysical possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as aerial/corporeal subtile bodies (apparitional substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scriptural contexts (disciples seeing Jesus on the sea, angels appearing) treat 'spirits' as aerial or subtle bodies—corporeal in the sense of occupying place (though finer) rather than mere phantasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple witnesses perceive a figure (not a private delirium) and Scripture attributes movement and visibility, favor reading the apparition as some kind of subtle corporeal substance rather than mere private fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angel as 'Messenger' (primary signification)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'angel' the Scripture most commonly means a messenger—anything that manifests God's extraordinary presence, especially by dream, vision, voice, or visible sign; not necessarily a permanent incorporeal being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpreting 'angel' passages, ask whether the text presents a voice, vision, pillar (cloud/fire), dream, or visible personification serving as a sign of God's presence. Treat such manifestations as 'angels' in the functional sense of messengers or signs rather than assume a fixed ontology without textual warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive evidence about angels' permanence/materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some New Testament and other texts (e.g., references to punishment prepared for 'the devil and his angels', judging angels, angels detained in chains) suggest angelic permanence and materiality rather than pure immateriality; therefore 'incorporeal' is not a safe universal assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh passages that imply angels are subject to judgment, punishment, and place (and thus not utterly immaterial) against others. Where the text ascribes everlasting fire or spatial punishment, prefer an interpretation that preserves angels' capacity to be affected (i.e., materiality or substantial existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration as metaphor for divine guidance of minds
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Inspiration' in Scripture should be read metaphorically: God inclining the minds of writers, granting prophetic dreams/visions, or signifying external tokens (e.g., wind at Pentecost), rather than the infusion of God's substance into men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literalizing inspiration as the transmission of divine substance. Read 'Scripture given by inspiration' as meaning God inclined or disposed the writers' minds toward the teachings useful for instruction, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. Distinguish prophetic dreaming/moving from the doctrine of infusion of deity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat supernatural signs as literal 'stuff' to be poured or infused
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'poured out' or 'given' (Joel, Pentecost) are metaphorical for granting prophetic gifts or graces, not literal effusions of divine substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Scripture speaks of God 'pouring out' spirit, read this as promising gifts (dreams, visions, prophecy, sanctifying graces) rather than a physical transfer. Treat spiritual 'gifts' as virtues or capacities rather than movable substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God primarily a literal covenantal polity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to much theological usage that makes 'kingdom of God' a purely metaphoric phrase for heavenly felicity, Scripture most commonly uses it to denote a real kingdom constituted by covenant (e.g., God's peculiar people under a pact), i.e., a civil sovereignty by pact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret references to the 'kingdom of God' in historical and covenantal contexts (e.g., Genesis-Abraham, Sinai renewal) as indicating God's civil sovereignty over a specific people by consent. Where New Testament texts claim restoration or political reign (e.g., Gabriel's words about the throne of David), read these as claims about real dominion, with political consequences (e.g., conflict with Caesar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs for identifying the 'kingdom' in Scripture (covenantal markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of covenantal acts (promise to Abraham, circumcision, Mosaic covenant at Sinai), sacral status ('peculiar people', 'holy nation'), priestly institutions, and explicit statements of God's reign over a people are markers that a text is speaking of a literal kingdom of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a passage refers to God's civil kingdom, look for explicit covenant language, institutions (sacraments, priesthood), and narrative acts of appointment or governance. Use such markers to distinguish metaphoric spiritual senses from claims about earthly polity.
